original_question: Does there exist any pair (n, d) for which the minimal exponent p needed to extend Delta^p Phi to all degree-d forms is strictly greater than 1?
target_in_paper: Section 5.2, Open Problem 5.5, stated explicitly as a subproblem of Open Problem 5.1: "Is there an example with p > 1?"
correct_elements: The draft correctly targets the paper’s Section 5 question about the exponent p attached to the associated-form morphism Φ, and it captures the right existential thrust: whether p can ever be strictly greater than 1 for some choice of n and d. It also correctly understands p as the minimal exponent needed to clear the discriminant denominator so that Δ^pΦ extends beyond the nondegenerate locus.
missing_details: The paper works with homogeneous degree-d forms in n variables over C, with n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 3.
The domain on which Φ is initially defined is X_n^d = {f ∈ C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d : Δ(f) ≠ 0}, the affine open set of nondegenerate forms.
Φ is not an arbitrary map: it is the associated-form morphism Φ: X_n^d → C[e_1, ..., e_n]_{n(d−2)} ≅ C[z_1^*, ..., z_n^*]_{n(d−2)}, defined in Section 2.1 by formulas (2.6) and (2.8).
Δ is the discriminant on the full affine space C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d of homogeneous degree-d forms.
The exponent should be named as p = p(n,d), the smallest positive integer such that Δ^pΦ extends to a regular morphism on the entire affine space C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d, not just on X_n^d.
The codomain of the extended morphism should be stated explicitly as forms of degree n(d−2) on the dual space.
The phrase "all degree-d forms" should be made precise as the full vector space C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d, including degenerate forms with Δ = 0.
refined_question: For integers n ≥ 2 and d ≥ 3, let X_n^d = {f ∈ C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d : Δ(f) ≠ 0}, let Φ: X_n^d → C[z_1^*, ..., z_n^*]_{n(d−2)} be the associated-form morphism, and let p = p(n,d) be the smallest positive integer such that the product Δ^pΦ extends to a regular morphism C[z_1, ..., z_n]_d → C[z_1^*, ..., z_n^*]_{n(d−2)}. Does there exist any pair (n,d) for which p(n,d) > 1?
justification: The draft is not aiming at Conjecture 1.1, but at the Section 5.2 problem about the contravariant Δ^pΦ. After defining p via the extension property of Δ^pΦ on the full affine space of degree-d forms, the paper first asks the broader Open Problem 5.1, "Compute the integer p," and then isolates exactly the user’s existential version as Open Problem 5.5, "Is there an example with p > 1?" This is therefore the nearest official formulation and should not be broadened to the full computation problem. The surrounding context that makes the question stand alone comes from the definition of X_n^d and the associated-form morphism in Section 2.1, the equivariance statement in Proposition 2.3, and the Section 5.2 definition of p together with Theorem 5.2 and Propositions 5.3–5.4, which explain why asking whether p can ever exceed 1 is a natural sharpened subproblem.
